script: He was "the old guy" who stole commissions—then he vanished. What happened next?. I was working in sales, and Bob was the old‑timer who made everyone's day a circus. He'd pull the rug out from under us, let customers bail, and then claim the commission. He was a legend to the managers because he'd been in the business forever, but to us he was pure annoyance. One day, I decided to give him a taste of his own medicine. I slipped into his cubicle, changed his screensaver to "Bob is a Jackass," and watched him type his password like he didn't know what was coming. He didn't notice until he was halfway through a call, then the banner rolled across the screen, and the office erupted in giggles. He was furious, of course. He stormed to the manager's desk, shouting about harassment, and the manager just laughed and told him to calm down. He even changed the screensaver himself—no big deal. A couple of hours later, another manager—Mr. Johnson—called me up. He was mad. "What the heck are you doing? This is a policy violation. You're not supposed to share passwords. Get out of here." He told me to leave the building and that I'd be suspended for three days. I walked out the back door, down the stairwell, and drove away. It was Wednesday, so that meant a five‑day weekend. I was stoked. On the way to my car, I could hear someone yelling, "Hey James, Peggy wants to see you." Peggy was the HR lady. I ignored it and drove in the opposite direction. Fifteen minutes later, my phone rang. I didn't answer; those minutes were expensive. I got home, told my wife we were getting a five‑day break, and we headed out to the beach about three‑and‑a‑half hours away. An hour later, my phone rang again. My wife begged me to pick up. I did. "Hey James, it's Peggy. I need you to sign some forms about the three‑day suspension." I said, "Sorry Peggy, I was told to leave. I am out of town. I'll sign later." She was not thrilled but I had no choice. Soon after, my direct supervisor called. "James, where are you? We need the numbers for this client coming in today. And you had the presentation stored on… Where are you?" He told me Mr. Johnson had sent me home for messing with Bob's screensaver. "No one told me. Why didn't you come down and tell me? Come back and give me the reports." I told him I'd already left town, that I couldn't share my password because I was told not to, and that I was over an hour away. He told me to be there first thing tomorrow. I told him I wouldn't be back until Monday because I'd been given three days off. He said, "You have to be kidding. He didn't mean three days." I turned my phone off—no smartphones, just a basic one, so that was fine. Sunday, I listened to the messages. My manager said Mr. Johnson didn't realize we had projects I was leading and that he wanted me back the next day. The next day, Mr. Johnson told me I could give my password just this time. He said leave. I left. He said no sharing. He said three days. For a company that never gave anyone a day off, that was a mini vacation. I came back to work on Monday. Nothing had changed. They moved the project around, they did the presentation, and I just made a sale. In sales, problems go away if you sell something. And that was the whole story: I was suspended for three days, I left town for a five‑day weekend, and the company just kept going.
